newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Japan seeks mediator role in global warming.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks mediator role in global warming.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who will host a global warming conference in Kyoto this year, tried on Monday to play the role of mediator in setting targets for cutting heat-trapping pollution.

In a speech at the "Earth Summit Plus Five" at the United Nations, Hashimoto called on world leaders to send a strong message to set "meaningful, equitable and realistic" targets for cutting emissions from burning fossil fuels.
"I assure you that Japan is resolved to do its utmost in this regard, and I sincerely appeal to all the countries gathered here to extend their cooperation to the Kyoto Conference," he said.
As host to the Kyoto global warming conference in December, Japan finds itself in the delicate position of wanting to take a mediating role without commiting to setting tough targets itself.

The special U.N. General Assembly session, designed to discuss progress in fighting global warming since the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago, is the last gathering of world leaders before the Kyoto meeting, which is aimed at seeking agreement on legally binding cuts in greenhouse gases.
Emissions of carbon dioxide are believed to heat the atmosphere with potentially dire consequences such as rising sea levels, severe weather and spread of tropical diseases.
"It is necessary that each of us develop a strong consciousness and shoulder our responsibilities. We must change our lifestyles," Hashimoto said.
Japan belongs to a group of countries led by the United States that do not want tough targets for curbing greenhouse gases, fearing harsh measures to slash pollution would devastate their economies.
The European Union proposed a 15 percent reduction in emissions below the 1990 level by 2010. Small island states wanted a much higher reduction.

"Japan maintains that discussion on the frameworks like how to fairly share costs is needed before setting targets. However, we will seek cooperation from countries to set numerical targets," a senior Japanese official accompanying Hashimoto said. "Japan wants to be a mediator," he said.

Hashimoto, who attended a Group of Seven summit in Denver that ended on Sunday, hailed a communique saying the economic superpowers wanted "meaningful, realistic and equitable" targets for curbing greenhouse gas emissions by 2010.
"This is a message addressed to this special session as well," he said. The communique disappointed European leaders, falling short of European Union calls for a substantial cut.

Hashimoto drew attention to other aspects of global warming by making proposals for Japan's enhanced role in developing energy-saving technologies and promoting the transfer of those technologies to developing countries.

He also pledged that Japan would give the "greatest possible consideration" to official development assistance, or foreign aid, in its efforts to preserve the environment despite severe budgetary constraints.

Tokyo's aid will be used to set up a network among East Asian countries to share data on acid deposits, promoting energy saving technology transfers, preventing water pollution and establishing a coral reef preservation study centre.
